oracle.evidence: recheck@4.5.0 (MIT), wired into the rule as an optional second stage and used as the grading oracle here. It analyses the automaton for exponential and polynomial ambiguity and returns a proof either way — unlike a search for an attack string, which has no `safe` verdict at all. Of 107 cases on the corpus it decides 102 and leaves 5 (all runtime-assembled).

effectiveFp.evidence: TECHNICAL false positives are 0 of 102 decided cases — every literal pattern still reported is proven superlinear by the oracle, and the 4 it proved safe are now retracted by the rule itself. Worst case including the 5 undecidable runtime-built cases is 4.7%, under the 5% bar. But EFFECTIVE FP is not this number: it also counts findings that are correct and that nobody would act on, and many of these are polynomial patterns on inputs the application may already bound (class E1 in FALSE-POSITIVE-CATALOGUE.md). That judgement has not been made for a single finding.

reachability.evidence: The rule asserts that a PATTERN is dangerous, never that attacker input reaches it. A catastrophic regex matched only against internal constants is not exploitable, and we report it identically. Partial reachability is achievable in-file — `re.test(req.body.x)` is visible — and would cut the finding count hard; full reachability is not, because a regex is usually exported and applied elsewhere (L1). This is a contract change, not a patch: it moves the claim from "this pattern is dangerous" to "this pattern is dangerously reachable", and that is a decision to take deliberately.
reachability.command: see FALSE-POSITIVE-CATALOGUE.md class E1 and ANALYSIS-LIMITS.md L1

corpus.evidence: MANIFEST.md: vulnerable/ holds patterns whose blow-up was MEASURED on V8 with the timings in each header; safe/ holds patterns that LOOK catastrophic and are provably linear. Written to ask whether the rule decides from the automaton or from the printed shape.

duel.evidence: 14 TP / 0 FP / 0 FN — 100.0% precision, 100.0% recall, 100.0% F1

adversarial.evidence: Two waves, 2026-08-18, both written after the rule reached 100% F1. Wave 1: 15 patterns the rule had never seen, labelled by TIMING via redos-classify (6 measured exponential, 9 unreproduced) — 6 of 6 caught, 0 missed. Wave 2 held the weakness constant and varied only the spelling: one measured-exponential automaton (x+x+)+y reached by 15 syntactic routes — 2 FALSE NEGATIVES (const R = RegExp; new R(p), and new globalThis.RegExp(p)) plus 2 FALSE POSITIVES (a parameter named RegExp, and a local shadow). All four fixed by resolving the intrinsic through the scope chain instead of matching callee.name; 0 of 15 now missed.

knownGaps.summary: 5 of 107 cases build their pattern at runtime from interpolated values, so no fixed automaton exists to analyse.
knownGaps.why: The oracle needs a pattern; these have a template. The verdict rests on values the file receives rather than defines — a column type from schema metadata, a package name, a deployment prefix. One of the five (webpack) interpolates a const declared in the same file, so it is resolvable in principle and the rule simply does not follow it.
knownGaps.reopenWhen: the rule resolves in-file constant interpolation, which would decide at least the webpack case

knownGaps.summary: Technical FP is 0; effective FP — would a developer act — has never been measured for this or any rule.
knownGaps.why: Open work, not a limit. A polynomial pattern on a field the application caps at 200 characters is a correct finding nobody would act on, and it counts against the 5% bar exactly as a wrong one does. Deciding it needs either real users or an agreed proxy.
knownGaps.reopenWhen: immediately — this is the industry's decisive gate and the only one never attempted

knownGaps.summary: Every finding claims the pattern is dangerous; none claims attacker input can reach it.
knownGaps.why: Open work AND a contract question. The in-file half is buildable — a regex applied to a visible request surface — and would likely take this rule well under the 5% bar on its own. The cross-file half is L1. Changing the claim is the kind of decision that should be taken once, deliberately, for the whole ecosystem rather than rule by rule.
knownGaps.reopenWhen: the ecosystem settles whether default-enabled rules assert reachability, which the README now says they must
